source.title: Feature Identification via the Empirical NTK

record.tranche_reason: The study analyzes grokking in modular-addition networks using eNTK feature-alignment measures, a different method from the original accuracy-based studies. It reports both generalization trajectories and how alignment with Fourier features changes during training.
record.gate_note: The Gemma-3-270M grammar-feature and PCA results concern feature identification, not grokking or delayed generalization, so they are not recorded as rows for these claim versions. The paper's discussion of earlier work is not treated as new evidence. Table 8's per-run, per-layer Fourier-overlap breakdown is omitted; its four reported test accuracies are retained.
record.test_reason: The paper's aim is eNTK feature identification, but it reports its own grokking trajectories for a 1L MLP and a 1L Transformer on modular addition. It also tracks a continuous measure: eNTK eigenspace alignment with the Fourier circuit features. That measure rises smoothly through training, and its derivative peaks near grokking onset. This is a different method aimed at V2's question, plus an incidental replication of V1's basic delay at a single train fraction.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is mostly right but too narrow. The main conclusion is that eNTK eigenanalysis can surface features across three settings: Fourier features in a modular-addition MLP and Transformer, and grammar features in Gemma-3-270M, where it beats a same-budget PCA baseline. Grokking appears as a secondary finding: subspace alignment grows rapidly near the transition, which may help monitor feature acquisition. The authors note the results are correlational, not causal.
record.recipe_differences: Uses modular-addition grokking setups, including a 1L MLP and a 1-layer Transformer, but the study's focus is eNTK feature alignment rather than reproducing grokking as its primary outcome. It does not test training-set-size scaling.
record.method_sensitivity: Transformer key Fourier frequencies are seed-dependent; eNTK spectra differ by layer, so the paper analyzes layerwise spectra. The reported temporal alignment results concern selected runs and layers.

fits_no_version.finding: In the Gemma-3-270M experiment, eNTK eigendirections recover part-of-speech and morphology features better than PCA. This is static feature identification with no training dynamics.

record.problems: The main results include a particular MLP run and a particular Transformer seed; robustness checks are reported, but Table 8's additional runs give only fixed-budget test accuracy and detailed layerwise overlaps. Temporal alignment results are described qualitatively or shown in figures without numerical uncertainty. The study does not test the training-set-size dependence in V1, and its alignment evidence is correlational.
record.rows_left_out: Appendix E.2, Table 8 reports layerwise Fourier overlaps for four additional Transformer runs. The per-run/per-layer breakdown was left out to keep the record focused on the main alignment results; the four test-accuracy values after 4000 epochs are included in r41-r44.

untested.parts: Dependence of the delay on training-set size: only one α per architecture (0.7 MLP, 0.5 Transformer) is reported with trajectories.
Later removal of memorizing components is not measured, and the timing of alignment is not compared against other progress measures.
Not tested: no non-algorithmic grokking, and no sweep of initialization scale or weight norm.
Not tested: Gemma-3-270M is used only for static feature identification, with no training trajectory.
Not tested: no critical dataset size or ungrokking.
Only incidental seed variation in key frequencies (see missing); there is no deliberate cross-architecture or hyperparameter test.
Not tested: no optimizer or numerical-precision controls.

missing.what: In the MLP, first-cliff eNTK eigendirections already overlap with the a and b Fourier modes at initialization. The paper attributes this to architecture and data symmetry. So part of the Fourier structure is present from the start rather than forming gradually, which qualifies V2's gradual-formation reading.

Across five Transformer seeds, the same Fourier-type algorithm appears at different seed-dependent key frequencies (4, 4, 2 and 3 frequencies; 2 in the main run). The layerwise pattern is reported as robust across seeds. This is weak evidence on V6: the same algorithm class with run-dependent details.
MLP robustness runs at (p=19, α=0.8), (p=23, α=0.75) and (p=31, α=0.65) report only eNTK spectra. No accuracy trajectories or delays are given, so they cannot speak to V1's dataset-size dependence.

record.verdict_notes: Many convergence-table rows were non-matching families or random controls marked 'absent'. That state would read as evidence against V2, so they were relinked to none. The V2 support is qualitative and figure-based: the derivative peaks at onset rather than clearly before it, and there is no uncertainty estimate and only one run per architecture for the trajectories. Nanda et al. (an original source) is used as the ground-truth algorithm reference; this study is not itself an original source.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not compare training-set sizes or test whether smaller training sets require more optimization.
It measures eNTK eigenspace alignment with Fourier features and its evolution, but does not directly track removal of memorizing components.
No non-algorithmic training data or initialization-scale/weight-norm sweep testing whether grokking-like delays can be switched on or off.
No LLM pretraining or fine-tuning trajectory for delayed generalization.
No test of an efficiency account, critical dataset size, or ungrokking.
No test of whether different runs converge to the same algorithm across architectures or hyperparameters.
No test of adaptive-optimizer instabilities or floating-point/softmax artifacts as an explanation of the delay.
